slides: Welcome back. The last part of the topic is scale.

slides.say: A map is a similar copy of the real world, only much smaller. So everything we learned about similarity works on maps.
The scale is a ratio. A length on the map, to the same length in reality.
Say the scale is one to fifty thousand. Every centimeter on the map is fifty thousand centimeters in reality.

slides: The map and the land are similar shapes, and the scale is their linear ratio. So every real length is fifty thousand times the length on the map.

slides.say: Fifty thousand centimeters isn't a useful distance. So we change the units, step by step, like on a ladder.
From centimeters to meters, we divide by a hundred, because a meter is a hundred centimeters.
From meters to kilometers, we divide by a thousand, because a kilometer is a thousand meters.
So fifty thousand centimeters is fifty thousand divided by a hundred, five hundred meters.
And five hundred meters is five hundred divided by a thousand, half a kilometer.
So on this map, one centimeter is half a kilometer in reality.
Now on numbers. On this map, two towns are six centimeters apart. How far apart are they really?
Every map centimeter is half a kilometer. So six centimeters are six halves, three kilometers.
And backwards. Two towns are really four kilometers apart. How far apart are they on the map?
One centimeter is half a kilometer, so each kilometer is two map centimeters. So four kilometers are four times two, eight centimeters.
Sometimes they give both distances, and ask for the scale. Say three kilometers in reality are six centimeters on the map.
First we write both in centimeters. Three kilometers are three thousand meters, and three thousand meters are three hundred thousand centimeters.
at: Three kilometers are three thousand meters

slides.say: So six map centimeters are three hundred thousand real centimeters. One map centimeter is three hundred thousand divided by six, fifty thousand.
So the scale is one to fifty thousand.

slides: And remember, a bigger number in the scale means a smaller map. On a scale of one to two hundred, a house is big. On one to fifty thousand, it's only a dot.

slides.say: Now areas. The map and the land are similar. So, like any similar shapes, the areas use the scale squared.

slides: Here's the easiest way. First change one map centimeter into the real unit they want. Then square it.

slides.say: On our map, one centimeter is half a kilometer. So one square centimeter on the map is a real square, half a kilometer by half a kilometer.
at: one square centimeter on the map

slides.say: Half times half is a quarter. So it's a quarter of a square kilometer.
So a lake of eight square centimeters on the map is eight quarters, two square kilometers.
Be careful here. A lot of students multiply eight by half a kilometer, and get four. That forgets to square.
Let's sum up. The scale is the linear ratio between the map and reality. Lengths are multiplied by the scale, and areas by the scale squared.
at: The scale is the linear ratio

slides.say: Change units with the ladder, step by step.
And for areas, change one map centimeter into the real unit first. Then square it.
